title: How Thoroughbred Horses Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how Thoroughbred horses work, prompted by the upcoming Breeders' Cup and Uncle Mo's favorite status, after Josh's trip to the Kentucky Derby and Preakness. They define horse terms (colt, filly, foal, yearling, sire, dam, stallion, broodmare, pony), then cover the breed's origins from three Oriental foundation sires (Byerly Turk, Darley Arabian, Godolphin Arabian) crossed with English mares; physical traits such as stride length, heart and spleen, and breathing; the General Stud Book and the Jockey Club's control of registry and naming; purses and the economics of racing; the January 1 birthdate convention; the harsh realities of breeding, injuries, and slaughter; the horse bubble; and a listener mail from Gauge asking about careers at HowStuffWorks.
topics: horse terminology colt filly foal yearling sire dam

segments.title: Opening banter and Breeders' Cup preview
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about Uncle Mo being the favorite for the Breeders' Cup at Churchill Downs, Josh's trip to the Kentucky Derby and Preakness, and how the article came about.

segments.title: Horse terminology
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh define horse terms: colt, filly, foal, yearling, sire, stallion, dam, broodmare, and pony.

segments.title: Oriental foundation sires and origins of the breed
segments.summary: The Thoroughbred was developed in England in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries from three Oriental stallions (Byerly Turk, Darley Arabian, Godolphin Arabian) bred with English mares. The Byerly Turk was captured in Hungary, the Darley Arabian was acquired by Thomas Darley and smuggled out of Syria and Turkey, and the Godolphin Arabian passed through France and eventually to the Earl of Godolphin.

segments.title: Thoroughbred traits: size, speed, stride, and physiology
segments.summary: Typical Thoroughbred size and lifespan are described, along with stride length (about 20 feet), stride rate, and the large heart and spleen that boost oxygen-carrying red blood cells while running. Horses breathe only through their nose, and their rear legs work like springs.

segments.title: General Stud Book and registry rules
segments.summary: All Thoroughbreds trace through the sire to the three foundation sires. James Weatherby created the General Stud Book, a closed registry. The Weatherby family and Jockey Club control registry and naming rules, and the American Stud Book starts in 1868. The Jersey Act of 1913 excluded many American horses until 1949.

segments.title: Purses, racing economics, and the age cutoff
segments.summary: Purses in the US exceeded a billion dollars in 2010 gross. Only a small share of foals win substantial purses, and very few win Grade One races. Racing careers are short. All Thoroughbreds share a January 1 birthdate for racing age, which creates an age disadvantage and leads to breeding interventions.

segments.title: Breeding practices, slaughter, and the horse bubble
segments.summary: Stallions are used for covering up to three mares a day, and unsuccessful horses may be slaughtered. Slaughter figures for Great Britain, the US shipping to Canada, and Canadian numbers are cited. The horse bubble saturated the market with foals, causing prices to fall and abandonment and slaughter to rise. Injuries to Barbaro and Eight Belles are mentioned, along with rescue organizations.

segments.title: Listener mail from Gauge
segments.summary: Gauge, a fifteen-year-old from Minnesota, asks about qualifications for a career as a neurologist writing for HowStuffWorks. The hosts suggest submitting a portfolio and possibly blogging for the show.

segments.title: Closing and promotions
segments.summary: The hosts mention a Thoroughbred documentary about the 2006 Kentucky Derby, point to the article for further reading, explain how to contact the show, and promote a video podcast.
